Field surveys along temperate sandy beaches of the southwestern Atlantic indicate that Amarilladesma mactroides reaches a maximum shell length of 8.5 centimeters [Li = 8.5 centimeters], a size that distinguishes it as one of the larger donacid bivalves in the region. This ultimate dimension is attained after several years of growth on dissipative shores characterized by fine to medium sand. Growth analyses based on annual ring counts from a sample of several hundred individuals suggest that the species approaches this asymptotic size gradually, with a marked deceleration in shell accretion after sexual maturation. The largest specimens are typically recovered from sub-tidal zones where food availability and hydrodynamic conditions favor sustained somatic investment. Given the commercial importance of this clam, the maximum recorded length provides a critical benchmark for fishery management, as size-based harvest regulations must protect individuals until they have had the opportunity to reproduce. The magnitude of this terminal shell length also influences local ecological interactions, as larger clams are less vulnerable to predation by epibenthic crabs and demersal fishes, thereby shaping the species' demographic structure within sandy beach assemblages.

Gonadal development in this species begins when individuals attain a shell length of approximately 4 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4 centimeters], marking the onset of reproductive maturity. Histological examinations of the gonads reveal that gametogenesis commences at this size threshold, with the first evidence of vitellogenic oocytes and spermatogenic follicles appearing in clams collected during the austral spring. The shell length at puberty appears to be remarkably consistent across populations from southern Brazil to northern Argentina, suggesting a strong genetic basis for this developmental milestone rather than purely environmental modulation. Individuals smaller than this length are invariably immature, exhibiting undifferentiated gonadal tissue. The transition to reproductive competence at four centimeters represents a critical life-history juncture, after which energy previously directed exclusively toward somatic growth becomes partitioned between continued shell accretion and gamete production. This allocation shift has implications for population dynamics, since the age at which clams reach this pivotal size determines the generation time and the potential for population recovery following harvest or natural disturbance events.

Reproductive output in the yellow clam is substantial, with females capable of releasing extraordinarily large numbers of gametes during a single spawning event. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], gravid individuals were observed to produce approximately 3,000 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 3,000 eggs per day] over the peak of the spawning period. This maximum reproductive rate is achieved only after females have reached their full adult size and is sustained for several weeks during the summer reproductive season. The daily fecundity was estimated by collecting spawned eggs from individually isolated clams maintained in flow-through seawater tanks, with counts performed using a Sedgewick-Rafter chamber. Such high fecundity is characteristic of broadcast-spawning bivalves that face high rates of larval mortality in the plankton. Fertilized eggs develop into free-swimming veliger larvae that drift in coastal currents for several weeks before settling. The prodigious numerical output at 17 °C compensates for the extensive losses incurred during the planktonic phase, ensuring that at least some larvae encounter suitable benthic habitat for metamorphosis.

The initial mass of newly released offspring is remarkably small, with the wet weight at birth measured at 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams], corresponding to an egg diameter of approximately 200 micrometers. This minute size places the yolk reserves of the embryo at the lower end of the range documented among donacid bivalves. Upon fertilization, the zygote develops rapidly through a lecithotrophic trochophore stage, relying entirely on endogenous yolk supplies for its energetic needs. The small birth mass imposes a tight constraint on the duration of the non-feeding larval phase, as the limited yolk must sustain development until the veliger larva acquires the capacity for phytoplankton ingestion. Field observations suggest that the transition to planktotrophic feeding occurs within 24 to 36 hours after hatching at typical seawater temperatures. The minuscule size of the newly hatched larva also renders it vulnerable to a wide array of planktivorous predators, including copepods, chaetognaths, and gelatinous zooplankton, making the early planktonic period a demographic bottleneck of considerable significance for population recruitment.

Adults of Amarilladesma mactroides achieve a maximum wet tissue weight of 11.6 grams [Wwi = 11.6 grams], representing the soft-body mass exclusive of the shell valves. This ultimate somatic mass is typically observed in clams that have reached or approached the maximum shell length (8.5 centimeters) [Li = 8.5 centimeters] and is correlated with the reproductive condition of the individual. The relationship between shell length and tissue weight follows a power-law function, with the majority of somatic growth occurring during the juvenile phase before the onset of gonadal maturation. At 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for this species is 6 years [am = 6 years], a relatively short duration compared to many other marine bivalves of comparable size. Longevity was determined through a combination of mark-recapture studies and analysis of shell micro-growth bands in individuals collected from a protected beach in southern Brazil. The 6-year lifespan at this thermal regime suggests that the species follows a relatively fast life-history pace, with rapid growth to maturity, high reproductive output, and early senescence. This life-history strategy is well-suited to the dynamic and unpredictable sandy beach environment, where disturbance from storms and shifting sediment can cause episodic mortality, favoring species that can quickly recolonize available habitat.
